**Hypothesis**: During the Younger Bronze Age (1100–500 BCE), the principal component value of PC1 at the beginning of the period (1100 BCE) represents the absolute zenith of prehistoric capital accumulation, reaching an all-time series high of **+4.45**, whereas the subsequent time horizons between 1000 and 500 BCE exhibit an immediate, steep collapse and sustained deflation down to a mean of **+1.44** (range: +0.82 to +2.17). 

This sharp difference reflects a structural transition from a hyper-concentrated climax of symbolic capital (daggers, large house sizes), social capital (copper/gold wealth, monument frequency), and economic capital (massive hoards/depots) at 1100 BCE, to an abrupt post-climax fragmentation and depletion of prestige metals and monumental display from 1000 BCE onward, despite high pottery decoration diversity persisting throughout the period.

payload.workflow: 1. Ingested capital.csv (100-year discrete archaeological time slices) with European comma decimal parsing. 2. Performed SVD-based PCA on the 12 forms of capital across 4300–500 BCE. 3. Evaluated component loadings and variance explained for PC1. 4. Extracted and compared YBA horizons (1100 BCE vs. 1000–500 BCE). 5. Performed sensitivity analysis with correlation-standardized PCA and isolated YBA subset.
payload.hypothesis: During the Younger Bronze Age (1100–500 BCE), PC1 at the beginning of the period (1100 BCE) reaches an unprecedented global maximum (+4.45), significantly exceeding all subsequent time horizons between 1000 and 500 BCE (mean: +1.44; range: +0.82 to +2.17), driven by an immediate post-1100 BCE collapse in copper/gold prestige metals, daggers, house sizes, and monument density, followed by the gradual depletion of metal hoards.
